analysis.one_liner: Authorizes the health secretary to ban evictions nationwide during disease outbreaks.
analysis.headline: Introduced a month after the Supreme Court blocked the CDC's eviction ban, the bill drew 56 Democratic cosponsors, no Republicans, and died in committee without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: During the COVID-19 pandemic, the CDC banned evictions to keep contagious people from being put out of their homes and crowding into new ones. The Supreme Court blocked that ban in August 2021, saying the law Congress wrote didn't give the CDC that power. This bill would have fixed the law: it would have written the eviction-ban power directly into the Public Health Service Act and required a nationwide eviction moratorium through the COVID emergency and 60 days after it ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters who fall behind on rent during a disease outbreak. The moratorium would have been automatic, with no application needed, and would have covered the whole eviction process, from the initial court filing through the final removal. Since losing a home spreads disease through crowding and displacement, renters and everyone around them benefit when eviction is paused during a public health emergency.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends Section 361 of the Public Health Service Act to state that federal health regulations may implement, maintain, or extend a residential eviction moratorium during disease outbreaks.
It requires the HHS Secretary to put a national eviction moratorium in place to slow the spread of COVID-19, one that stays in effect at least 60 days after the public health emergency ends.

The moratorium would be automatic, without requiring individuals to apply, and would cover eviction filings, hearings, judgments, and execution of judgments, with narrow exceptions the Secretary could create to protect health and safety.

analysis.who_pays: Landlords and rental property owners. A moratorium stops them from evicting tenants who stop paying rent while the landlords still owe mortgages, taxes, and upkeep, and the bill contains no federal mechanism to reimburse them for rent owed during the ban. Smaller owners with thin cash margins bear this hardest; large corporate landlords can absorb it.

drawbacks.text: The moratorium covers all eviction filings, hearings, judgments, and removals, so a landlord who keeps paying the mortgage, taxes, and maintenance on a unit may collect no rent for months. The bill provides no federal reimbursement or rental-assistance mechanism for that gap, a burden that falls hardest on small owners rather than large corporate ones.

The bill is a direct response to the Supreme Court's August 2021 ruling that the CDC's earlier eviction ban exceeded the agency's legal authority. Supporters of the ruling argued that a blanket federal freeze on evictions reaches too far into matters traditionally governed by state landlord-tenant law; this bill answers that argument by writing the power explicitly into federal statute rather than narrowing the policy.

A moratorium stops evictions but does not erase the rent owed. Tenants who stay through the moratorium can emerge with months of accumulated rental debt that may still lead to eviction or collections later.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit is large and concrete: keeping people housed during a contagious-disease emergency protects both the household and everyone around it, and the automatic nationwide coverage means no one has to navigate an application to be protected. The cost is also real: landlords keep their obligations but lose their remedy when tenants don't pay, and because the bill pairs no payment mechanism with the ban, the strain lands on property owners, especially small ones. A better-designed version would have tied the moratorium to rental assistance so neither renters nor landlords carry the whole cost; this bill did not, which was its most honest weakness.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, sent to its Health subcommittee, and never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: The CDC had banned residential evictions during the COVID-19 pandemic under its interpretation of existing law, but the order faced multiple legal challenges, and the Supreme Court blocked enforcement of the most recent order on August 26, 2021.

Rep. Cori Bush introduced the bill on September 21, 2021, with 40 original cosponsors, to give the HHS Secretary clear statutory authority for eviction moratoria and to mandate a nationwide COVID-19 moratorium.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on September 21, 2021, and to the Health subcommittee the next day, where the record ends.
Fifty-six House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.
The House never considered the bill, and the CDC's own eviction moratorium ended in 2021; the bill expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Landlords and property owners, who faced no new federal eviction ban and kept the ability to remove tenants for nonpayment, and the House leadership that kept the bill off the agenda. Renters had no federal eviction protection through the end of the emergency.

for.name: Rep. Cori Bush
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to restore statutory authority for federal eviction moratoria after the Supreme Court struck down the CDC's ban.

against.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill before the committee; after referral to the Health subcommittee, no markup, hearing, or vote ever occurred.

against.name: Supreme Court of the United States
against.what_they_did: Blocked enforcement of the CDC's eviction moratorium on August 26, 2021, ruling it exceeded the agency's statutory authority, which removed the protection the bill sought to restore.

against.name: Landlord and real estate trade associations
against.what_they_did: Challenged the CDC eviction order in court and opposed federal eviction moratoria, leading to the legal rulings that the bill aimed to answer.

sides.party_line_note: All 56 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican sponsored or supported the bill, though the bill never reached a floor vote so no roll call exists.

industries.note: A moratorium would bar them from evicting tenants who stop paying rent during a health emergency, while they still owe mortgages, taxes, and maintenance. Their financial interest runs against renters' interest in keeping their homes, and the bill offered them no reimbursement.

industries.industry: Residential real estate trade associations and property management firms
industries.note: These groups challenged the CDC moratorium in court and opposed statutory revival of eviction bans. Large corporate owners can absorb uncollected rent better than small landlords, so within the industry the burden of a moratorium falls unevenly.
